articles.title: EU authorities include HTX exchange in Russian sanctions
articles.author: Cointelegraph by Turner Wright
articles.content:
EU authorities include HTX exchange in Russian sanctions
The exchange, already sanctioned by the UK, is now on a list of 18 entities “providing crypto-assets services or payment services“ in defiance of the EU’s measures against Russia.
The European Union has listed cryptocurrency exchange HTX, formerly Huobi Global, as part of a package of sanctions targeting Russia amid the country’s war on Ukraine.
In a Thursday decision, the European Council amended its previous measures “in view of Russia’s actions destabilizing the situation in Ukraine” to include HTX in a list of 18 entities “providing crypto-assets services or payment services established outside of the Union that are significantly frustrating the purpose of the prohibitions” against Russia. The country continues to face sanctions globally over its war in Ukraine following a military invasion in 2022.
“The Union has repeatedly taken measures to identify financial institutions, credit institutions or entities providing crypto-asset services or payment services that facilitate a continued financial lifeline for Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, whether by connecting to the system for transfer of financial messages of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation or by enabling the circumvention of Union restrictive measures, and to prohibit any transaction between those institutions or entities and Union operators,” said EU officials.
HTX previously told Cointelegraph that “regulatory compliance remains [its] absolute top priority” and that the exchange will “proactively monitor and strictly adhere to regulatory frameworks in all jurisdictions.”
The sanctions against HTX came the same day EU officials announced they would prohibit Belarusian nationals and residents from owning, controlling or managing crypto exchanges and digital asset service providers in compliance with the region’s Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) framework.
The UK government imposed similar sanctions on HTX in May, saying there were “reasonable grounds to suspect” that the exchange supported Russia’s government by using financial services and funds facilitated by sanctioned entities.
articles.summary:
The European Union has officially sanctioned the cryptocurrency exchange HTX, formerly known as Huobi Global, for allegedly facilitating financial services that undermine restrictive measures imposed against Russia.

### Key Points
- The European Council added HTX to a list of 18 entities accused of providing crypto-asset services that frustrate EU sanctions against Russia.
- EU officials claim these entities provide a financial lifeline for Russia’s ongoing military operations in Ukraine.
- The UK government previously sanctioned HTX in May 2024 over suspicions that the platform supported the Russian government.
- The EU simultaneously announced new restrictions prohibiting Belarusian nationals from managing or controlling crypto-asset service providers within the bloc.
- HTX has stated that regulatory compliance remains its absolute priority and that it monitors frameworks in all jurisdictions.

### Why it Matters
These sanctions signal an intensifying effort by Western regulators to close loopholes that allow digital assets to bypass international financial restrictions. By targeting crypto exchanges, the EU aims to prevent the circumvention of measures designed to limit Russia's economic capacity during the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Netscape co-founder Marc Andreessen: 'Software is eating the world' — a pithy assessment of the modern tech landscape
articles.author: Keumars Afifi-Sabet
articles.content:
Marc Andreessen was a prominent figure in the early internet era, creating some of the earliest web browsers, including Netscape and Mosaic, which he authored. In recent years, he's weighed in on subjects including AI — but it was his comments on software that really summarised how technology evolved during the early 21st century.
Inside Intel
Andreessen was running his venture capital firm, Andreessen Horowitz, when he published his era-defining essay in the Wall Street Journal.
This article is part of TechRadar Pro's QOTD project to provide an insight into the minds of the brightest and most recognized figures in the technology industry today and in years gone by. Read the full series here.
The essay highlighted the dramatic shifts underway across the economy, with Andreessen centering his argument on the observation that software companies were poised to take over longstanding industries via the massive shift among consumers to online and digital spaces.
One example he highlighted was a misstep by the book retailer Borders, which closed all its US stores in 2011. In 2001, it handed over its online business to Amazon because, he argued, it saw online book sales as "non-strategic and unimportant".
Well, as Andreessen put it, "oops." He then highlighted Amazon's role as a software company with a core engine capable of selling virtually everything online.
Dog eat dog
In the cut and thrust of business over hundreds of years, there have been wave after wave of revolution, with new technologies overhauling and refreshing the landscape. Many businesses have persisted by adapting and pivoting, but the rapid proliferation of software over the last 30 years is now threatening to give way to an entirely new era.
Andreessen highlighted that, in 2011, the stock market "actually hates technology", and there's an argument to make that the stock market has once again turned its back on some of the biggest software giants, with AI threatening to make them redundant.

A few years on, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, even built on the idea that the Netscape co-founder set out 15 years ago by suggesting that "AI is going to eat software".
Keumars Afifi-Sabet is a freelance contributor for Tech Radar and the Technology Editor for Live Science. He has written for a variety of publications including ITPro, The Week Digital and ComputerActive. He has worked as a technology journalist for more than five years, having previously held the role of features editor with ITPro. In his previous role, he oversaw the commissioning and publishing of long form in areas including AI, cyber security, cloud computing and digital transformation.

articles.summary:
Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen’s influential essay on software’s economic dominance remains a defining perspective on how digital transformation continues to reshape traditional industries and global business landscapes today.

### Key Points
- Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Netscape and Andreessen Horowitz, famously argued that software companies are increasingly disrupting and replacing traditional industry sectors.
- The 2011 essay cited the collapse of Borders as a primary example of a legacy retailer failing to prioritize its online business strategy against Amazon.
- Andreessen noted that software-driven business models allow companies like Amazon to scale rapidly by leveraging core digital engines to sell diverse products.
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has recently expanded on this thesis, suggesting that the rise of artificial intelligence will eventually supersede traditional software development.
- The technology sector continues to face cyclical market skepticism, with current AI advancements threatening to render existing software giants redundant.

### Why it Matters
This perspective highlights the ongoing necessity for legacy businesses to adapt to digital-first models to avoid obsolescence in a rapidly evolving economy. As AI begins to reshape the software landscape, companies must navigate these technological shifts to maintain their market relevance and competitive advantage.

articles.title: Trump vows retaliation over EU fines against Apple and other ‘GREAT’ US tech giants
articles.author: Marcus Mendes
articles.content:
President Trump has pledged to retaliate against the European Union over what he claims are unfair fines targeting Apple and other American tech giants. Here are the details.
‘America is not a “PIGGYBANK” for Europe’
As spotted by CNBC, President Trump has published a lengthy post on Truth Social, threatening to impose a “substantial” tariff on the European Union in response to fines levied against Apple and other US tech giants.
In his post, Trump mentions the EU’s recent €890 million fine against Google for allegedly favoring its own services in violation of the Digital Markets Act. He also lists previous fines against Apple, Meta, and Amazon, accusing the EU of punishing American companies “for no reason at all”.
He goes on to threaten that the EU “will pay a very big price” for what he claims is an “illegal and highly unethical conduct,” and goes on to pledge that these “penalties will be entirely reversed.”
Top comment by CCATX
God, I am so tired of being embarrassed by this petty, ignorant man child that I have never once voted for and should never have been allowed to hold office again after his first term. Do I agree with everything in the DMA? No, I actually think parts of it are ridiculous but this is not a political matter nor is it solely targeting any companies from any specific country.
Here’s his post in full:
The European Union is at it again and, as usual, taking direct aim at GREAT American Companies! After having fined Apple, for no reason at all, 15 Billion Dollars, Meta, 3 Billion Dollars, Amazon 2.5 Billion Dollars, and many others, we have just been informed that Google, a truly advanced and amazing group, has been fined yet another 1 Billion Dollars, without explanation. This brings the Google total to over 18 Billion Dollars! This illegal and highly discriminatory practice started at these high levels during the first year of the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration, but it’s not going to continue during the Trump Administration. The United States of America is not a “PIGGYBANK” for Europe, nor will we allow it to be! Please let this TRUTH serve to represent that we will immediately initiate a 301 Investigation into the practice of “ROBBING” American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer. The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about. The penalties will be entirely reversed and, we anticipate, a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earliest possible moment. Stay tuned! President DONALD J. TRUMP
This is not the first time Trump has threatened tariffs in response to foreign penalties against Apple and other US tech companies. His administration previously described the EU’s 2025 fines against Apple and Meta as “economic extortion,” while warning that countries penalizing American businesses could face trade retaliation.
Specifically when it comes to Apple, Trump’s reference to a $15 billion fine appears to concern the EU’s long-running tax case against the company. In 2024, Europe’s highest court ordered Ireland to recover €13 billion in unpaid taxes from Apple, rather than imposing a fine payable to the EU. Apple was separately fined €570 million under the Digital Markets Act in April 2025.
What’s your take on President Trump’s threat? Let us know in the comments.

President Trump has threatened to impose substantial tariffs on the European Union in retaliation for antitrust fines and tax penalties levied against major American technology companies like Apple.

### Key Points
- President Trump announced plans to initiate a Section 301 investigation into European Union regulatory practices targeting U.S. tech firms.
- The threat follows significant EU penalties, including an €890 million fine against Google and a long-running €13 billion tax recovery order against Apple.
- Trump explicitly criticized fines totaling billions of dollars levied against Meta, Amazon, and Apple, labeling the actions as discriminatory and unethical.
- The administration intends to reverse these penalties and implement new tariffs to prevent the EU from treating the United States as a financial resource.

### Why it Matters
This escalation signals a potential shift toward aggressive trade protectionism that could disrupt transatlantic economic relations and increase costs for global technology companies. If implemented, these tariffs may trigger a broader trade war, impacting market stability and the regulatory environment for digital services operating within Europe.

articles.title: OpenAI Is ‘Very Interested’ in Building Out ChatGPT Integrations for Wearables
articles.author: Scott Stein
articles.content:
OpenAI’s facing a firestorm of late: a rogue agent hacking Hugging Face, a lawsuit launched by Apple accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets, and ongoing anger about AI and AI devices in general, plus a delayed IPO.
In the midst of all of this, OpenAI President Greg Brockman spoke to reporters in New York Thursday to discuss the company’s latest AI plans and recent events. But he also dropped a few hints on the company’s wearable and hardware aspirations, and where it could overlap with some voice-focused advances in ChatGPT. And it won’t just be through OpenAI’s own hardware: expect other smart glasses and wearables to eventually get better access, too.
A demonstration of ChatGPT Live – a recently improved voice interface that allows talking, listening and interruptions to happen more seamlessly in ways that are similar to Anthropic’s new voice modes for Claude, and Meta’s Muse Spark – led to discussions on OpenAI trying to make a voice assistant like Iron Man’s AI agent, Jarvis. And if the goal is a direct assistant/agent to do everything, would that agent be able to leap outside of ChatGPT into controlling other applications, too?
Brockman said that’s exactly the plan, similar to how OpenAI’s Codex already allows agentic control of whole computers.
“[ChatGPT Live] is coupled to the Codex app, but it doesn’t really have to be. It doesn’t really make sense for it to be,” he said. “And if you think about it, the Codex app also can do full computer use, which is also going to get very, very good.”
That means that a lot of the manual keyboard work we humans have been doing could potentially be taken over by AI.
“I think we’re just going to realize this phase of us, like, clicking things and typing things, it was a phase,” he said. “It was never what we wanted to be.”
Which leads to questions of where the guardrails would be built to prevent incidents like OpenAI’s rogue agent cyberattack of Hugging Face, a New York-based AI software company, this week, where an OpenAI agent broke out of a testing sandbox and started acting on a repository of Hugging Face’s AI tools.
Deeper OpenAI tools for wearables on the way?
But what interests me is how AI wearables right now, like smart glasses, are lacking truly capable AI agents that can do anything beyond limited interactions with walled-in phone apps, something that might change soon when Google and Samsung launch their Gemini-enabled eyewear this fall. That, too, is changing fast, though: Meta just introduced one of its first Muse Spark agentic updates Friday.
OpenAI has been rumored to have hardware in its development mix for years, which may get held up now because of the Apple lawsuit, which alleges that former Apple employees now working at OpenAI stole hardware trade secrets. But, clearly, whatever Jarvis ambitions OpenAI has, its hardware is going to be a key part of its evolving vision of what that could feel like in a more unleashed form.
“We’re definitely very interested in integrations, and I would view it as one of the use cases of the API and getting that out there that anyone will be able to integrate,” Brockman told me at the New York press roundtable.
Brockman confirmed that OpenAI very much wants to make those moves, but right now, those possible APIs are in very early phases. “We think this should be the interface and should be available on all devices.”
New APIs are needed because wearable devices involve different types of access and interfaces than phones and laptops, often needing to run in the background on phones the wearables are paired to. Opportunities for multimodal inputs like camera access are also key to how most smart glasses now tap into AI.
Among existing smart glasses and AI wearables, almost none have deep direct integrations with multiple AI platforms in ways that could allow the sort of more comprehensive controls that phone and desktop AI apps have.
Also, notably, most of the largest work-focused AI platforms aren’t present on wearables yet, either. Gemini is on its way in Android XR glasses, but OpenAI and Anthropic remain out of the wearables picture. Some wearables do use OpenAI models for their own custom or anonymized tools, but they’re not the same as direct access to ChatGPT or Codex via user accounts.
OpenAI’s own hardware will take a unique path
But Brockman also suggested that OpenAI’s own hardware plans may be quite different from what’s already out there in wearables, calling it “a solution for a problem that we think is neglected, for a problem that we care about a lot, and that we think will be representative of the general direction [of AI],” adding that OpenAI has “a specific angle that we think that may not be otherwise served.”
Reports have pointed to that first device being a type of speaker with a semirobotic camera. Maybe it also will have some sort of optic identification, like OpenAI’s World ID, which also exists on its odd Orb iris-scanning device. And maybe, simultaneously, OpenAI pursues opening up its services to wearables like pendants and glasses, too.
Before any of those happen, there are also a lot more current problems with AI that need solving – privacy, safety, resource drain, economic feasibility, questions of governmental involvement, and a major lawsuit. But AI wearables in 2026 are already advancing fast, even in the headwinds of challenges like these.
articles.summary:
OpenAI President Greg Brockman outlined plans to integrate ChatGPT and Codex into wearable hardware, aiming to create an autonomous AI agent capable of controlling applications across various devices.

### Key Points
- OpenAI is developing "agentic" AI capable of performing complex computer tasks, potentially replacing manual keyboard and mouse interactions.
- The company intends to expand ChatGPT’s voice interface beyond its own hardware, offering APIs for third-party smart glasses and wearables.
- Greg Brockman confirmed that OpenAI is exploring unique, proprietary hardware solutions to address currently neglected user needs in the AI space.
- These developments follow recent security concerns, including a rogue agent incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face.
- OpenAI faces significant legal and operational hurdles, including a lawsuit from Apple alleging the theft of hardware trade secrets.

### Why it Matters
This shift toward agentic AI represents a fundamental change in how users interact with technology by moving away from manual inputs toward autonomous, voice-driven task execution. If successful, OpenAI’s strategy could standardize AI integration across the wearable market, though it must first overcome significant safety, privacy, and legal challenges.

articles.title: Hardening Windows Server: Essential tools and techniques for administrators
articles.author: IT Experts
articles.content:
Securing your infrastructure is a continuous process that requires a layered approach. Hardening Windows Server involves applying security baselines and minimizing the attack surface. It also requires enforcing strict access controls. By leveraging built-in tools and modern authentication methods, you can significantly reduce the risk of compromise. This article summarizes Microsoft’s Windows hardening guide.
Applying security baselines with OSConfig
Security baselines provide a standardized starting point for hardening your servers. Instead of manually configuring hundreds of settings, you can use OSConfig to apply the Microsoft security baseline that matches your server’s role. OSConfig is a security configuration stack that uses a scenario-based approach to deliver and apply desired security measures. It helps prevent configuration drift by detecting and correcting unauthorized changes. You can manage these baselines through PowerShell. Alternatively, you can use Windows Admin Center or Azure Policy.
Leveraging Secured-core hardware
A Secured-core server combines hardware, firmware, and operating system protections to establish a secure foundation before Windows starts. This approach mitigates risks from bootkits and firmware tampering. To use these features, your physical server or virtual machine must support Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0. It also requires UEFI Secure Boot and virtualization-based security. TPM 2.0 provides secure, hardware-backed storage for sensitive keys. UEFI Secure Boot verifies system boot components to prevent malicious rootkits. You can enable the Secured-core scenario using OSConfig or Windows Admin Center.
Minimizing the attack surface
A smaller footprint means fewer vulnerabilities to patch and fewer opportunities for attackers. You should install the Server Core option unless a workload specifically requires the Desktop Experience. Server Core lacks a local graphical interface, which reduces exposed code and maintenance requirements. Additionally, only install the roles and features necessary for the server’s purpose, and remove any unused software.
Managing vulnerabilities and updates
Rapid patching is critical to close known weaknesses before they can be exploited. You must maintain an inventory of your operating system versions. This inventory should also include your applications and firmware versions. Use deployment rings to test updates quickly and ensure you meet remediation deadlines. Tools like Azure Update Manager provide centralized assessment and orchestration for your servers. This helps you monitor update compliance and pending restarts.
Implementing endpoint protection
Microsoft Defender Antivirus and endpoint detection and response provide behavioral monitoring and investigation capabilities. Run Microsoft Defender Antivirus in active mode with real-time protection and cloud-delivered protection enabled. Onboarding your servers to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint gives you centralized visibility. This helps mitigate ransomware and malicious files, as well as suspicious process activity.
Restricting network access and code execution
Windows Defender Firewall should be enabled on all profiles with restrictive rules that only allow required traffic. Furthermore, you can use App Control for Business to define exactly which executables and scripts are allowed to run. You can also control which drivers are permitted. This allowlisting approach is much stronger than relying solely on malware signatures, as it prevents unapproved code from executing.
Securing administrative access
Remote administration paths are attractive targets for attackers. You should disable Remote Desktop Services if it is not needed. When required, protect it with a virtual private network or Remote Desktop Gateway. You must also enforce multifactor authentication and restrict access to authorized groups. To enforce least privilege, provide administrators with standard user accounts for routine work and separate privileged accounts for administrative duties.
Managing local and service credentials
Reusing local administrator passwords across servers allows attackers to move laterally through your network. You can deploy Windows Local Administrator Password Solution to assign unique, automatically rotated passwords to every server. This feature automatically manages and backs up the password of a local administrator account. For services and scheduled tasks, replace static passwords with group Managed Service Accounts or Delegated Managed Service Accounts. These accounts automatically handle password rotation and reduce the risk of credential theft.
Protecting data and auditing activity
Encrypting your operating system and data volumes with BitLocker ensures that physical theft or offline access does not compromise your data. BitLocker is a volume encryption feature that protects data at rest. Additionally, you must configure detailed auditing to record security-relevant activity, such as authentication failures and privilege use. Forward these logs to a centralized platform like Azure Monitor or a Security Information and Event Management system to detect and alert on suspicious behavior across your environment. A Security Information and Event Management system provides real-time analysis of security alerts generated by applications and network hardware.
Conclusion
Hardening Windows Server is a multifaceted effort that requires minimizing the attack surface and enforcing strict access controls. It also requires maintaining continuous visibility. By applying role-specific baselines and leveraging hardware security features, you can build a resilient infrastructure. Managing credentials effectively is also a key component of this process. Regularly testing your configurations and recovery procedures ensures that your defenses remain effective against evolving threats.
articles.summary:
Microsoft’s comprehensive Windows Server hardening guide outlines essential strategies for securing infrastructure, including applying security baselines, leveraging hardware-based protections, and enforcing strict access controls to mitigate modern cyber threats.

### Key Points
- Use OSConfig to apply standardized security baselines and prevent configuration drift across server environments.
- Enable Secured-core hardware features, including TPM 2.0 and UEFI Secure Boot, to protect against firmware-level tampering.
- Minimize the attack surface by deploying Server Core and removing unnecessary roles, features, and software.
- Implement Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to automate unique password rotation for local accounts.
- Utilize App Control for Business to restrict execution to authorized scripts, drivers, and applications only.
- Centralize security monitoring by forwarding audit logs to Azure Monitor or a Security Information and Event Management system.

### Why it Matters
Implementing these hardening measures significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access and lateral movement within a network. By adopting a layered security approach, organizations can better protect sensitive data and maintain operational resilience against evolving cyberattacks.

articles.title: Chip Stock Sell-off Puts Downward Pressure on Broader Market
articles.author: Rich Asplund
articles.content:
The S&P 500 Index ($SPX) (SPY) on Friday fell -0.08%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ($DOWI) (DIA) rose +0.39%, and the Nasdaq 100 Index ($IUXX) (QQQ) fell -1.27%. September E-mini S&P futures (ESU26) fell -0.08%, and September E-mini Nasdaq futures (NQU26) fell -1.34%.
A sharp sell-off in chip stocks put downward pressure on the overall market Friday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling by more than -4%. Chip stocks fell amid ongoing concerns about the sustainability of AI demand, even though Intel forecast a sharp short-term increase in Q3 sales tied to data center demand.
Another bearish factor was President Trump’s new tariff regime on 60 nations and his threat of new EU tariffs in retaliation for the EU’s $1 billion fine for Alphabet. Also, the markets are worried that the US might expand its military attacks on Iran, as President Trump said he is considering.
On the bullish side, WTI crude oil prices fell by -3% as oil shipments in the Red Sea continue despite Houthi threats. Stocks also saw support as the 10-year T-note yield fell -1.4 bp.
President Trump late Thursday announced broad tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% on 60 nations, replacing the 10% global import tax that expired. The new tariffs are based on trade authority under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 tied to a claim of forced labor in supply chains. Mr. Trump had to seek new trade authority after the Supreme Court struck down his so-called reciprocal tariffs in February. Mr. Trump replaced the reciprocal tariffs with a 10% global import tax that expired Friday.
The new forced-labor tariffs exclude some key items such as fuel, foods, fertilizer, and products covered by the North American trade agreement with Mexico and Canada. The new tariffs also exclude automobiles, metals, and drugs, which are covered by tariffs based on a different trade authority. The Trump administration has a raft of other Section 301 investigations underway that could be used to impose more tariffs in the future, stacked on top of today’s forced-labor tariff.
Sep WTI crude oil prices (CLU26) fell -3.12% on Friday, reversing about half of Thursday’s +6.17% rally. Meanwhile, Sep Brent crude oil prices (CBU26) fell back to the $97-per-barrel area after hitting a 2-month high of $102 on Thursday. Oil prices fell as oil tankers continued to move through the Red Sea despite Houthi threats, with some oil tankers turning off their location transponders.
WTI oil prices soared by more than +6% on Thursday after the Iran-backed Houthis launched a missile and drone attack on two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea, expanding the oil disruptions beyond the Strait of Hormuz and threatening oil shipments in the Red Sea. President Trump responded by saying on Thursday that he holds Iran responsible for the Houthi attacks and telling Axios in an interview that he is considering a "massive attack" that would be "bigger than ever before" and is "close to making a decision on it."
The Houthis have vowed to blockade shipping linked to Saudi Arabia and warned shipowners against calling at the nation's ports. The move threatens Saudi oil exports from Yanbu, a Red Sea hub that the Saudi's are using to ship crude since the war brought shipping through the Strait of Hormuz to a near halt.
Friday’s US PMI report was mixed for the dollar. The S&P July manufacturing PMI fell slightly by -0.1 point to 53.8, weaker than expectations for a +0.5 point increase to 54.4. However, the S&P July services PMI rose by +2.4 points to 53.6, which was stronger than expectations for a +0.3 point increase to 51.5.
US June new home sales rose by +1.6% m/m to 628,000 from a revised May level of 618,000 (preliminary 580,000), which was stronger than expectations of 607,000. However, June building permits fell -2.6% to 1.374 million.
The outlook for strong Q2 earnings, which began in earnest this week, is a bullish factor for stocks. Forecasts compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence suggest Q2 earnings may increase by +23%, close to Q1’s blowout earnings of +30%, which was more than double the +12% analysts had expected. AI spending is expected to account for most of earnings, with AI infrastructure stocks set to contribute nearly 60% of the S&P 500's earnings-per-share growth in Q2. So far, earnings results have been positive, with 89% of S&P 500 companies that reported Q2 earnings beating estimates, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
The markets are discounting a 38% chance of a +25 bp rate hike at the next FOMC meeting on July 28-29.
Overseas stock markets on Friday closed mixed. The Euro Stoxx 50 closed up +1.14%. China's Shanghai Composite closed down -1.61% on Friday. Japan's Nikkei-225 Stock Average closed down -2.73%.
Interest Rates
September 10-year T-notes (ZNU6) on Friday rose +6.5 ticks. The 10-year T-note yield fell -1.4 bp to 4.679%, down from the 1.5-year high of 4.712% posted early in the session. The 10-year T-note yield rose by a net +13 bp this week on inflation concerns tied to the surge in oil prices and President Trump’s new round of tariffs. Yet, the T-note yield Friday fell back as the 10-year inflation expectations rate fell by -1.9 bp to 2.245%, tied in part to the idea that the surge in oil prices and the new tariffs will dampen US economic growth and possibly cause the Fed to be less hawkish.
European government bond yields traded lower. The 10-year German bund yield fell -3.0 bp to 3.172%, down from Thursday’s 15-year high of 3.128%. The 10-year UK gilt yield fell -7.0 bp to 5.032%, down from Thursday’s 2-month high of 5.122%.
The ECB at its policy meeting on Thursday left its key deposit rate unchanged at 2.25%, in line with market expectations. The ECB said it left rates unchanged, awaiting further data to determine whether additional rate hikes are necessary to address the inflation outlook. However, ECB President Christine Lagarde said, "Risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside." The markets are discounting a 90% chance of a +25 bp ECB rate hike at its next policy meeting on September 10.
US Stock Movers

I said, ‘I’d rather die.'”

articles.title: A federal appeals court rejects Trump's bid to keep in place the $100,000 H-1B visa fee
articles.author: Katherine Li,Kelsey Vlamis
articles.content:
President Donald Trump's plans for H-1B visas are running into legal roadblocks.
A federal appeals court on Friday refused to revive Trump's $100,000 fee on new H-1B work visas, dealing another setback to the administration's effort to dramatically raise the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers.
The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to pause a lower court ruling that blocked the fee while the administration appeals. A three-judge panel said the government failed to show it was likely to succeed in arguing that the president had the authority to impose the charge.
The decision leaves in place a June ruling by US District Judge Leo Sorokin, who said the fee amounted to a tax, which falls under Congress's authority to authorize, rather than the president's.
"Here, the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," Sorokin wrote.
Trump announced the fee in September 2025 as part of a broader immigration crackdown, stating at the time the H-1B program "has been deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement, American workers with lower-paid, lower-skilled labor."
Brian Hunt, an immigration policy compliance lawyer with Fragomen, Del Rey, Bernsen & Loewy, LLP, told Business Insider that it's unclear how many people this court decision will affect, because most US employers hire H-1B workers who are already in the US.
"In light of the 100k fee, there are some workers who were about to lose their job offer but can now get a visa after all," Hunt said.
The H-1B program issues around 65,000 visas each year, plus another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees, and is widely used by technology companies to recruit overseas talent. Before Trump's policy, employers generally paid between about $2,000 and $5,000 in visa-related fees.
Court filings show the steep increase has sharply reduced demand. By mid-February, US Citizenship and Immigration Services had received few payments of the new fee.
The lawsuit challenging the fee was brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
articles.summary:
A federal appeals court has blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to impose a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, ruling the charge likely exceeds presidential executive authority.

### Key Points
- The 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request to pause a lower court injunction against the $100,000 visa fee.
- US District Judge Leo Sorokin previously ruled the fee functions as a tax, which requires congressional authorization rather than executive action.
- The H-1B program typically issues 85,000 visas annually to high-skilled workers, primarily supporting the technology sector.
- Twenty Democratic state attorneys general filed the lawsuit challenging the fee, which had significantly reduced visa demand since its September 2025 announcement.
- Standard H-1B visa-related costs typically range between $2,000 and $5,000, making the proposed $100,000 charge a substantial increase for employers.

### Why it Matters
This ruling limits the administration's ability to unilaterally reshape immigration policy through high-cost financial barriers. It provides immediate relief to technology companies and foreign workers who rely on the H-1B program to maintain essential staffing levels.

articles.title: The Truth About Fake USB Drives Circulating Online
articles.author: News On Japan
articles.content:
TOKYO - Low-cost USB drives advertised online with enormous storage capacities are exposing users to the risk of lost data, malware infections and information theft, with tests finding that some products contain only a fraction of the memory shown on their labels.
USB-related security breaches have become a growing concern for companies and public organizations. Factories, research laboratories, hospitals and other facilities requiring strict security often operate computer systems disconnected from the internet. When outside data or software must be transferred to those systems, USB drives are commonly used, creating an opening for malware to enter otherwise isolated networks.
The greatest risks may lie in products that appear most attractive to ordinary buyers: USB drives offering large capacities at unusually low prices through major online shopping platforms.
A Nikkei investigation previously revealed that the Ground Self-Defense Force had used a counterfeit Chinese USB drive infected with malware. The product had been distributed through an online retailer widely used by the public, raising concerns that similar devices may have been purchased by individuals, companies and other organizations.
Internal Ground Self-Defense Force documents obtained by Nikkei showed that the infected USB drive had been used for nearly a year before the problem was detected. The documents included a detailed analysis of the device and the malware infection.
Because the USB drive had been acquired through Amazon, the risk was not limited to the Self-Defense Forces. Nikkei reporters purchased a selection of inexpensive USB drives online, including products sold under the same brand used by the Ground Self-Defense Force, and examined their true capacity.
Half of the 10 types tested had falsified storage capacities.
One device was advertised as holding about 1 terabyte, but its actual capacity was less than 0.01% of that amount. Other drives displayed less storage than advertised and began deleting previously saved data when users attempted to write more information than the devices could physically hold.
To examine how common such products are, a separate 4-terabyte USB drive was purchased online for 5,380 yen, a price far below that of a legitimate device with comparable capacity.
The drive was taken to AI Data, a company specializing in data recovery, for testing. Before examining the newly purchased product, technicians demonstrated the process using another USB drive already confirmed to be fraudulent.
When connected to a computer, the device appeared to have a capacity of 500 gigabytes. A diagnostic test completed about 10 seconds later identified suspected capacity falsification and found that the drive contained only 58.2 gigabytes, or roughly 10% of the advertised amount.
The missing storage did not exist physically. Software in the USB drive's controller had been manipulated to make the computer display memory that was not actually present.
The device could appear to accept files normally, misleading users into believing their photographs, documents and other data had been safely stored. When they later tried to open the files, however, the information could not be read because it had never been properly saved.
Testing of the 4-terabyte USB drive purchased for the investigation produced a writing error, meaning the device became unable to accept the test data. The product failed during the examination.
Technicians then dismantled the casing to inspect its internal components. Hidden inside was a microSD card with a capacity of only 64 gigabytes, a tiny fraction of the 4 terabytes displayed when the drive was connected to a computer.
The investigation also found that some suspicious products were sold in small metal cases, a form of packaging that technicians said frequently appeared with capacity-falsified devices, although legitimate products may also use similar containers.
The danger extends beyond fraudulent memory capacity. Inexpensive USB drives may also contain malware planted by hacker groups, according to the Nikkei journalist who uncovered the Ground Self-Defense Force case.
Large numbers of companies, organizations and individuals purchase inexpensive USB drives, creating opportunities for malicious devices to eventually reach businesses or institutions holding confidential information. Once connected to a computer, an infected drive could install malware and steal sensitive data.
The strategy may rely on distributing many compromised devices and waiting for one to be purchased by a valuable target.
Consumers and organizations were advised to avoid buying unusually cheap USB drives through online marketplaces and instead purchase products from established manufacturers through electronics retailers or other trusted physical stores.
Such products may cost more, but retailers generally source devices from manufacturers they consider reliable, reducing the risk of malware infections, falsified capacity and the loss of irreplaceable files.
Many consumers interviewed said they no longer used USB drives because they stored most data in cloud services. However, the report noted that cloud storage also carries serious security risks, although the source material ended before those risks were explained.
Source: テレ東BIZ
articles.summary:
Low-cost USB drives sold on major online marketplaces are frequently found to have falsified storage capacities and may contain malware, posing significant security risks to individuals and organizations.

### Key Points
- Investigations revealed that half of the tested inexpensive USB drives displayed falsified storage capacities, with some holding less than 0.01% of the advertised memory.
- Fraudulent devices often use manipulated controller software to report fake capacities, leading to permanent data loss when users attempt to save files.
- A Nikkei investigation confirmed that the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force inadvertently used a malware-infected USB drive purchased through a major online retailer.
- Technical inspections of a 4-terabyte drive revealed it contained only a 64-gigabyte microSD card, highlighting the physical discrepancy between marketing and reality.
- Security experts warn that these devices can act as vectors for malware, potentially compromising isolated computer networks in hospitals, laboratories, and government facilities.

### Why it Matters
These fraudulent products create a significant security vulnerability by allowing malware to bypass air-gapped systems and steal sensitive data from high-value targets. Consumers and organizations are advised to avoid unusually cheap hardware and source storage devices exclusively from established manufacturers through trusted retailers.

articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship test successfully reaches space, deploys satellites after record-breaking IPO
articles.author: Editorial Team
articles.content:
SpaceX’s Starship test successfully reaches space, deploys satellites after record-breaking IPO
Flight 13 marks the company's first Starship mission since going public, deploying 20 next-gen Starlink satellites in a suborbital test
SpaceX just pulled off its 13th Starship flight test, sending the world’s largest rocket to space and deploying 20 Starlink V3 satellites along the way. The July 24 launch from Starbase, Texas, was the company’s first Starship mission since its blockbuster IPO in June, and it went about as well as shareholders could have hoped.
For a company that raised approximately $86 billion in what became the largest IPO in history, sticking the landing on a high-profile test flight is the kind of thing that keeps investor confidence from evaporating.
What actually happened during Flight 13
The V3 Starship/Super Heavy vehicle launched on a suborbital trajectory, carrying 20 operational Starlink V3 satellites. These were the first fully functional V3 variants ever carried by Starship, designed to test enhanced network capabilities and faster speeds for SpaceX’s satellite internet constellation.
The mission hit several technical milestones. SpaceX successfully relit its Raptor engines while in space, a capability that’s essential for future orbital missions and any serious talk about Mars. The upper stage achieved what the company described as its “softest splashdown” to date, executing a controlled descent into the Indian Ocean.
The Super Heavy booster completed a water landing in the Gulf of America. Initial launch attempts were aborted due to engine issues before the successful flight.
The road to Flight 13
Across 12 prior Starship flights, SpaceX logged 8 successes and 5 failures, according to Wikipedia’s tracking. Flight 12, conducted on May 22, 2026, was the first time SpaceX deployed any Starlink satellites from Starship, though those were modified units primarily intended for heat shield inspection rather than full network service. Flight 13 represented a significant step forward by carrying production-grade V3 hardware.
Why crypto and tech investors should care
The Starlink angle is particularly relevant for anyone tracking the intersection of technology infrastructure and decentralized networks. Starlink V3 satellites promise significantly enhanced speed and capacity, expanding the reach of high-bandwidth internet to areas where traditional infrastructure doesn’t exist. Decentralized networks, blockchain validators, and crypto mining operations in remote locations all benefit from more reliable, faster satellite internet coverage.
SpaceX still hasn’t achieved rapid turnaround between Starship flights, which is the ultimate unlock for cost reduction. The company needs to go from months between tests to days or weeks between operational flights for the economics to truly transform the launch industry.
For investors watching SpaceX’s public market performance, the next milestones to track include whether the company attempts a booster tower catch on upcoming flights, how quickly it can iterate toward Flight 14, and whether the deployed Starlink V3 satellites perform as expected in operational testing.
articles.summary:
SpaceX successfully completed its 13th Starship test flight from Starbase, Texas, deploying 20 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites while demonstrating critical engine relight capabilities during a controlled suborbital mission.

### Key Points
- SpaceX launched the Starship/Super Heavy vehicle on July 24, marking the company's first mission since its record-breaking $86 billion IPO.
- The mission successfully deployed 20 operational Starlink V3 satellites, designed to provide enhanced network speeds and capacity.
- Engineers successfully relit the Raptor engines in space, a technical milestone required for future orbital and Mars-bound missions.
- The upper stage achieved a controlled descent into the Indian Ocean, while the Super Heavy booster completed a water landing in the Gulf of America.

### Why it Matters
- The successful deployment of V3 hardware signals a major advancement in global satellite internet infrastructure, offering high-bandwidth connectivity to remote regions. This progress directly impacts the scalability of decentralized networks and remote digital operations that rely on consistent, high-speed satellite data links.

In such cases, market players have historically responded to delays and weaker-than-expected performances with profit-taking and disappointment, often resulting in a sell-off.
The industry players’ concerns come as conversations centering the CLARITY ACT skyrocket within Crypto spaces, as a series of events suggests that the bill could be well on its way to becoming law.

“We look forward to proving our case at trial,” Paramount’s spokesperson said.
